# A Introduction — Extraction Digest
**Range:** raw lines 974–1609
**Source:** Nogalski, *The Book of Micah* (NICOT 2024)
**Coverage:** Cache file read in full (local L1–L636; raw ≈ 974–1609). Body Introduction I–VII plus endnotes 1–58.

## Claims

### C-A-01 — Three-phase compositional model (headline)
**Locus:** raw L976–L981 (I. Historical Backgrounds, opening)
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah’s early core of prophetic material deals with events in the latter part of the eighth century BCE. The second phase of the development of the book of Micah likely occurred in the aftermath of Jerusalem’s destruction… editors incorporated chapters 6–7… Finally, a later anthology (chapters 4–5) incorporates hopeful eschatological perspectives"
**Claim:** Nogalski argues Micah took final shape over a long period in three main developmental phases: (1) early core (eighth-century material, chs. 1–3 focus); (2) post-587 updates (chs. 6–7, sixth–fifth centuries) blaming leadership/people for 587 and adding a salvific ending (7:8–20); (3) later anthology (chs. 4–5) with hopeful eschatology for postexilic Jerusalem and the nations.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]], [[jerusalem]], [[remnant]]

### C-A-02 — Early core keyed to 722 and 701
**Locus:** raw L986–L988 (A. Eighth-Century Background)
**Quote/anchor:** "chapters 1–3 focus on two events from that period: (1) the fall of Samaria in 722 BCE, and (2) events surrounding the siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE by the Assyrian king Sennacherib"
**Claim:** Nogalski locates the early core’s historical horizon in Samaria’s fall (722) and Sennacherib’s siege of Jerusalem (701), both under Hezekiah’s reign (approx. 725–696 BCE on Nogalski’s preferred dating).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[samaria]], [[jerusalem]], [[sennacherib]], [[hezekiah]]

### C-A-03 — Samaria as rhetorical warning to Judah
**Locus:** raw L988–L989
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah 1:5–7 specifically mentions Samaria’s destruction as a warning to Judah and Jerusalem that they will suffer the same fate if they do not change their behavior."
**Claim:** Per Nogalski, Mic 1:5–7 uses Samaria’s destruction rhetorically as a warning that Jerusalem/Judah face the same fate absent reform; chs. 1–3 do not name the Assyrians explicitly but condemn behavior anticipating Assyrian subjugation and Sennacherib’s siege.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[samaria]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-A-04 — Superscription vs. datable early material
**Locus:** raw L990–L992
**Quote/anchor:** "Even though the superscription of Micah (1:1) dates Micah’s prophetic activity during the reign of three Judean kings (Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah), scholars seldom date texts in the book to the time of Jotham or Ahaz."
**Claim:** Nogalski reports scholarly practice of anchoring eighth-century materials primarily in Hezekiah’s reign (Samaria 722; Sennacherib 701), not Jotham or Ahaz—unless one accepts Ahaz’s death at 715 BCE.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[hezekiah]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-A-05 — Shephelah villages and 1:8–16
**Locus:** raw L992–L994
**Quote/anchor:** "These actions prove dangerous for villages in the Shephelah… Micah 1:8–16 presents the prophet’s message of destruction for those villages."
**Claim:** Nogalski links Hezekiah’s late-eighth-century resource-consolidation and defensive preparation to danger for Shephelah villages on Sennacherib’s march route; Mic 1:8–16 voices destruction for those villages.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[hezekiah]], [[sennacherib]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-A-06 — Jerusalem expansion under Hezekiah
**Locus:** raw L995–L997
**Quote/anchor:** "during the reign of Hezekiah, Jerusalem itself nearly doubled in size… including the arrival of refugees who fled to Jerusalem after the Assyrians defeated Samaria as well as broader population shifts caused by the upheaval of Assyrian rule"
**Claim:** Nogalski reports Jerusalem’s near-doubling under Hezekiah, with explanations including Samaria refugees and Assyrian-driven population exchanges; biblical reports credit wall extension, Siloam tunnel, storehouses, Philistine wars, and religious reforms (2 Kgs 18–20; 2 Chr 29–32).
**Wiki targets:** [[hezekiah]], [[jerusalem]], [[samaria]]

### C-A-07 — Mic 1–3 critique: elites, not Hezekiah by name
**Locus:** raw L999–L1003
**Quote/anchor:** "Mic 1–3 does not, however, focus attention on Hezekiah’s contributions to the city. Rather, Mic 1–3 critiques the nation for abandoning Yahweh (1:5–9) and for the injustice perpetrated by the wealthy over others."
**Claim:** Nogalski argues chs. 2–3 condemn greedy elites seizing land under fortification/centralization pressures; leaders, prophets, and priests exploit rather than restrain oppression (3:1, 5–7, 11); climax is Jerusalem’s destruction in 3:12. Hezekiah is not named, but Nogalski suspects royal orders or tacit support.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[hezekiah]], [[jerusalem]]

**Locus:** raw L1003

**Claim:** Nogalski attributes insertions/explanatory comments in Mic 1:5–7, 9, 12, 13 to the second (post-587) phase explaining Jerusalem’s destruction.

### C-A-09 — Four accounts of Sennacherib’s siege
**Locus:** raw L1007–L1011
**Quote/anchor:** "We possess four accounts of these events, but the details differ among them: three biblical accounts (2 Kgs 18:13–19:37; 2 Chr 32:1–22; Isa 36:1–37:38); and Sennacherib’s own account."
**Claim:** Nogalski notes four divergent accounts: three biblical (sharing a common source, each altered for literary setting) ending with a divinely sent plague forcing Assyrian withdrawal; Sennacherib’s account credits Hezekiah’s rebellion (capture of Padi), tribute payment, Padi’s reinstatement, and division of Judean territory among loyal Philistine kings—without massive Assyrian casualties.
**Wiki targets:** [[sennacherib]], [[hezekiah]], [[isaiah]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-A-10 — Biblical vs. historical aftermath of 701
**Locus:** raw L1012–L1014
**Quote/anchor:** "the biblical accounts imply that Sennacherib was killed immediately after he returned from his campaign against Jerusalem. In reality, while Sennacherib was eventually assassinated by two of his sons, he continued to rule for another twenty years"
**Claim:** Nogalski contrasts biblical implication of immediate post-siege death of Sennacherib with historical rule ~20 more years before assassination by two sons; Hezekiah retained a reduced kingdom after 701.
**Wiki targets:** [[sennacherib]], [[hezekiah]]

### C-A-11 — Manasseh, delayed judgment, Chronicler’s solution
**Locus:** raw L1015–L1018
**Quote/anchor:** "the destruction of Jerusalem does not happen for more than fifty years after Manasseh died. The Chronicler tries to solve the problem by eliminating 2 Kgs 21:10–15… and inserting a narrative detailing Manasseh’s radical conversion"
**Claim:** Nogalski frames Manasseh’s long reign (696–641) and Kings’ prophetic judgment oracle (2 Kgs 21:12–13) as dual theodicy problems (why no removal; why delay until after Manasseh); Chronicler removes the oracle and adds conversion (2 Chr 33:11–17, 19).
**Wiki targets:** [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-A-12 — Josiah to 587 narrative arc
**Locus:** raw L1020–L1097 (approx. local L41–L117)
**Quote/anchor:** "Josiah becomes the paradigm of a pious king… In 605 BCE Babylon defeated Egypt at the Battle of Carchemish… Nebuchadnezzar razed the city"
**Claim:** Nogalski surveys Amon’s assassination; Josiah’s reforms (Book of the Law / Deuteronomy-related); Neco II and succession Jehoahaz→Jehoiakim; Carchemish 605 and Nebuchadnezzar II; conflicting deportation-year tables (2 Kgs / Jer 52 / 2 Chr); Jehoiakim’s revolt, Jehoiachin’s 597 deportation, Zedekiah’s revolt and 587 razing of wall, houses, temple, palace, and metal furnishings.
**Wiki targets:** [[jerusalem]], [[james-nogalski]]

### C-A-13 — After 587: landscape and Zion failure
**Locus:** raw L1099–L1106
**Quote/anchor:** "With the events of 587, all three pillars of Zion theology had failed. There was no longer a Davidide on the throne; Jerusalem lay in ruins; and Babylon demolished and looted the temple. Nevertheless, Zion theology did not die. It adapted."
**Claim:** Nogalski states 587 ended Davidic rule (after 400+ years), destroyed temple/personnel structures, and shifted administration to Mizpah under Gedaliah (assassinated after ~two months); Zion theology’s three pillars failed but adapted rather than died.
**Wiki targets:** [[jerusalem]], [[micah]], [[remnant]]

### C-A-14 — Mic 4–7 as adaptive Zion response
**Locus:** raw L1107–L1109
**Quote/anchor:** "First, chapters 6–7 clarify that Yahweh initiated the destruction of Jerusalem in response to poor leadership and the sins of the people of Judah. Second, 7:8–20 provides a message of hope… Finally, someone compiled an extensive unit in chapters 4–5 that functions as a prophetic articulation of Yahweh’s future plan for Zion."
**Claim:** Nogalski maps Mic 4–7 additions (first at Mizpah, later near reconstructed temple/city) as: blame (6–7; 6:1–7:7), remnant hope (7:8–20; Exodus analogy), and future Zion plan (4–5); cites Mic 4:10–12 (Zion to Babylon, then redemption; nations gathered against Zion without knowing Yahweh’s plan).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[jerusalem]], [[remnant]]

### C-A-15 — Postexilic readers and verified promises
**Locus:** raw L1134–L1137
**Quote/anchor:** "the postexilic community knows the veracity of most of the promises already. The postexilic community can know that Assyria and Babylon have fallen… people have begun returning from Babylon."
**Claim:** Nogalski argues that placing chs. 4–5 in an eighth-century-set book lets postexilic readers treat partially fulfilled promises (Assyria/Babylon fallen; return begun) as grounds for confidence that remaining eschatological Zion restoration will follow.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[remnant]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-A-16 — Unity: three major blocks
**Locus:** raw L1140–L1143 (II. Unity of Composition)
**Quote/anchor:** "Three or four major divisions are often noted: (1) the early core appearing in Mic 1–3… (2) Mic 6–7… and (3) chapters 4–5, which vacillate between judgment and hope"
**Claim:** Nogalski describes Micah as a thoughtfully arranged collection not wholly from the named prophet: early core (1–3: social inequity and cultic impropriety); 6–7 (trial/guilt 6:1–7:7 + multi-voice optimism 7:8–20); 4–5 (judgment/hope toward distant future).
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

Shephelah); superscription kings Jotham (756–741), Ahaz (741–725), Hezekiah (725–696); Micah as youngest of four eighth-century prophets with Isaiah, Hosea, Amos; presupposes 722 and 701.

### C-A-18 — Sixth-century updates: Hos influence and parity with North
**Locus:** raw L1159–L1163
**Quote/anchor:** "This chapter repeatedly equates the religious behavior of Jerusalem to Samaria and classifies gifts to other deities as money paid to a harlot (Mic 1:5–7, 9a, 12b, 13b)… The harlotry language reflects influence of Hos 1–3"
**Claim:** Nogalski attributes sixth-century insertions in Mic 1 (1:5b, 9; new sense of 1:12–13) and comparable material in 6–7 to laying blame for 587; Jerusalem paralleled with Samaria/Omri–Ahab (6:16); “Israel” language for Judah; knowledge of Hosea and Amos as Northern condemnations assumed.

### C-A-19 — 7:1–7 complaint and 7:8–20 liturgy
**Locus:** raw L1164–L1165
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah 7:8–20 has often been classified as a liturgy because of the speaker and response style… The climactic moment in the liturgy comes with the prophet’s intercessory prayer in 7:14–15a followed by Yahweh’s brief but positive promise"
**Claim:** Nogalski presents 7:1–7 as prophetic complaint (disappearance of faithful/upright) and 7:8–20 as Persian-period salvific ending/liturgy climaxing in intercession (7:14–15a), Yahweh’s promise (7:15b), and people’s grateful proclamation.

### C-A-20 — Chs. 4–5 postexilic topics and Isaiah-like portrait
**Locus:** raw L1171–L1173
**Quote/anchor:** "These chapters presuppose knowledge of the exile to Babylon (see esp. 4:10)… They also reflect an eschatological orientation… Hence, they do not come from the eighth century. The cumulative effect… characterizes Micah as a prophet in the vein of Isaiah"
**Claim:** Nogalski dates bulk of 4–5 postexilic: temple and nations (4:1–5), remnant (4:6–7; 5:7–8), Zion dominion (4:8–13), Davidic continuation (5:1–6), cultic purification (5:9–14); day formulas at 4:1, 6; 5:10; effect is an eighth-century prophet whose book addresses the postexilic community, analogous to Isaiah.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[isaiah]], [[remnant]], [[jerusalem]]

### C-A-21 — Zion reconstitution vs. blame (4–5 vs. 6–7)
**Locus:** raw L1175–L1177

**Claim:** Nogalski contrasts 4–5 (reassert Zion city, Davidic leadership, protection; nations’ pilgrimage for torah/word; peace; remnant defeats nations; cultic cleansing) with 6–7’s blame focus; 4:1 follows jarringly after 3:12 (Masoretes mark 3:12 as exact middle of the Twelve by verses).

### C-A-22 — Scribal prophets and themes of the Twelve
**Locus:** raw L1179–L1181
**Quote/anchor:** "Recent suggestions have highlighted the likelihood that a group of scribal prophets are responsible for shaping the books comprising the Latter Prophets… conceptual elements include… chronological structure… day of Yahweh… fertility of the land… fate of God’s people… theodicy."
**Claim:** Nogalski attributes 4–5 (and broader shaping) to scribal prophetic education; postexilic funding shifts from king to temple; recurring Twelve themes include chronology (eighth century–Persian), day of Yahweh, land fertility as covenant sign, people’s fate over time, and theodicy.

### C-A-23 — Moresheth / Moresheth-Gath identification
**Locus:** raw L1189–L1191 (III. Authorship and Place of Origin)

**Claim:** Nogalski reports traditional scholarly identification of Micah’s hometown as Tell-el-Judeideh (~20+ miles SW of Jerusalem); 1:9–16 warns Shephelah cities on Assyria’s path; Sennacherib claims 46 fortified Judean cities destroyed.

### C-A-25 — Stable Hebrew transmission, no major pluses/minuses
**Locus:** raw L1209–L1212 (IV. The Text of Micah)
**Quote/anchor:** "The text of Micah, unlike that of Jeremiah or Ezekiel, does not exhibit significant pluses or minuses when compared to early manuscript traditions in Hebrew and Greek."
**Claim:** Nogalski judges Micah’s Hebrew transmission relatively stable (like much of the Twelve); complexities are mostly comprehension of unpointed poetry by scribes/translators, not large structural differences among MT, LXX, Qumran, and Judean Desert texts.

### C-A-28 — 8Ḥev 1 / Mic 5:4(3) and same Vorlage
**Locus:** raw L1219–L1287
**Quote/anchor:** "Despite the very different meanings of Greek words in the LXX and 8Ḥev 1, both translations interpret the same unpointed Hebrew text."
**Claim:** Nogalski uses first-century CE Greek Twelve MS 8Ḥev 1 (Nahal Hever; nothing after Mic 5:6) to show: Mic 5:4 not in Qumran/Murabbaʿat Hebrew fragments but present in 8Ḥev 1 (not a late addition); LXX vs. 8Ḥev 1 differences (extra “see”/flock paraphrase; yšb vs. šûb for wyšbw; kyrios vs. paleo-Hebrew YHWH) reflect alternative translations of one Hebrew base, not a different Vorlage.
**Wiki targets:** [[micah]], [[james-nogalski]], [[nogalski-micah-nicot]]

### C-A-29 — Commentary text-critical method
**Locus:** raw L1292–L1301
**Quote/anchor:** "They highlight the stability of the unpointed text of the Twelve and demonstrate a certain fluidity in the copying and translation of texts… lack of clarity does not, however, suggest the translators were working with a text significantly different from MT in the case of Micah."
**Claim:** Nogalski states principles for selective text notes: err toward inclusion of variants (incl. Greek synonyms without different Vorlage); note paleo-Hebrew YHWH practice; scribes generally succeeded in accurate Micah transmission.

### C-A-30 — Micah sixth in MT; third eighth-century superscription
**Locus:** raw L1307–L1322 (V. Reading Micah in the Twelve)
**Quote/anchor:** "In the MT (and English Bibles), Micah appears as the sixth book… the third and final prophetic collection in the Twelve whose superscription dates the prophet to the eighth century."
**Claim:** Nogalski: Twelve = Hosea–Malachi on one scroll, one of four Latter Prophets; MT order intentional; Hosea–Amos–Micah superscriptions pattern eighth-century kings (Jeroboam II for North in Hosea/Amos); Hezekiah in Mic 1:1 is great-great-grandfather of Zephaniah (Zeph 1:1); six king-dated writings span eighth–sixth centuries.

### C-A-31 — Intellectual background: Neh 9:32; 2 Kgs 17; Isa 10
**Locus:** raw L1324–L1351

**Claim:** Nogalski frames Micah amid: Ezra’s prayer dating hardship “since the time of the kings of Assyria until today” (Neh 9:32); 2 Kgs 17’s Israel-then-Judah warning paralleling Mic 1; Isa 10’s Assyria as “rod of my anger” then punished after work on Zion—linking Sennacherib-siege plague motif.

### C-A-32 — Jonah–Micah–Nahum and Assyria
**Locus:** raw L1352–L1359
**Quote/anchor:** "Micah provides the linchpin connecting the deliverance of Nineveh in Jonah and Nineveh’s destruction in Nahum because, in Micah, the Assyrians act with malice toward Judah and they destroy Samaria."
**Claim:** Nogalski: in MT order Micah sits between Jonah (Nineveh repents/survives) and Nahum (Nineveh doomed); Micah shows Assyrian malice and Samaria’s fall; ancient interpreters ordered Jonah before Nahum (mercy then reversion to evil); judgment/hope alternation structures prophetic books.

### C-A-33 — Sirach 49:10 and early unity of the Twelve
**Locus:** raw L1361

**Claim:** Nogalski counters MS-only objections to Twelve coherence: Judean Desert MSS ~mid-second century BCE lack a collection title, but Sir 49:10 already treats the Twelve as a prophetic book with Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel.

### C-A-34 — Book of the Four (Hosea–Amos–Micah–Zephaniah)
**Locus:** raw L1362–L1365
**Quote/anchor:** "the sequence of Hosea, Amos, Micah, and Zephaniah can hardly be accidental. They always appear in the same order relative to one another even when one factors in the Septuagint order"

### C-A-37 — Mic 6:6–8 as trial dialogue and ḥesed
**Locus:** raw L1380–L1384
**Quote/anchor:** "the prophet’s response in 6:8 basically accepts the opponent’s claim that Yahweh does not need blood sacrifice, but that the opponent has ignored a deeper guilt… he has failed 'to do justice, to love kindness [ḥesed], and to walk modestly with … God.'"
**Claim:** Nogalski: 6:6–8 assumes two speakers—opponent (1st person, Yahweh in 3rd) interrupts trial speech with hyperbolic sacrifice questions; 6:8 is prophet (not Yahweh) answering ʾādām; justice/ḥesed/love language denser in Hosea/Amos than Micah; Hos 12:6 nearly parallels the triad; sequential Micah has not yet stated ḥesed until 7:18, 20.

**Claim:** Nogalski distinguishes NT uses of Mic 5:2 (Matt 2:5–6; Luke 2:15; John 7:40–42) affirming Jesus as Messiah from original OT intent: Davidic figure delivering from siege and restoring exiles; OT context is foundational for interpretation.

### C-A-39 — Themes for modern reception
**Locus:** raw L1394–L1399

### C-A-41 — Analysis of Contents outline (structure)

### C-A-42 — Note on scholarly diversity re: dating later materials
**Locus:** raw L1496–L1497 (n. 1)
**Quote/anchor:** "no consensus exists on the precise dating of the later materials… Andersen and Freedman… prefer that Micah was revised before the Persian period… Utzschneider… 4:1–5 comes from the Hellenistic period… 6:9–16 and 7:1–7… Persian period"
**Claim:** Nogalski cites Andersen/Freedman (not all eighth-century; possible Ezra-era edit or pre-Persian revision) and Utzschneider (dramatic two acts; 2:6–12 Jeremianic; 4:1–5 Hellenistic; 6:9–16; 7:1–7 Persian fifth–fourth centuries) to show long history of composite-reading without consensus on dates.

**Locus:** raw L1532–L1533 (n. 19)
**Quote/anchor:** "there remains a significant pattern of recognizing the three parts of Micah (chs. 1–3, 4–5, and 6–7)… Andersen and Freedman… imply that Mic 6–7 entered after chs. 4–5… completed in the early part of the Persian period at the latest."
**Claim:** Nogalski reports majority view that 1–3 is early (with possible later editing of 1:1, 5–7, 9, 12, 13; 2:12–13); three-part pattern widely recognized; Andersen/Freedman order 4–5 then 6–7, finish by early Persian at latest—Nogalski’s own model puts 6–7 (exilic/sixth-century blame + Persian ending) before postexilic 4–5 reframing.

### C-A-46 — LXX order of the Twelve derives from MT sequence
**Locus:** raw L1580–L1581 (n. 43)
**Quote/anchor:** "This rearrangement suggests that the Septuagint order represents a sequence of writings that derive from the MT and not the other way around."
**Claim:** Nogalski: two main sequences (MT/English vs. LXX); LXX groups Hosea–Amos–Micah first (eighth-century emphasis) then Joel–Obadiah–Jonah as in MT, then Nahum–Malachi as MT—read as rearrangement from MT, not source of MT.
**Wiki targets:** [[book-of-the-twelve]], [[hosea]], [[amos]], [[micah]], [[jonah]]

### C-A-47 — Chronological placement of remaining Twelve books
**Locus:** raw L1584–L1585 (n. 45)
**Quote/anchor:** "Jonah… would logically fit between Amos and Micah… Nahum deals with the fall of the Assyrian Empire… Habakkuk assumes Yahweh’s sending of Babylon… Only Joel and Obadiah do not explicitly owe their position to chronology."
**Claim:** Nogalski explains MT placement logic: Jonah (Jeroboam II via 2 Kgs 14:25) between Amos and Micah; Nahum (612 Nineveh) + Habakkuk (Babylon) fill gap before Zephaniah; Malachi after Zechariah (rebuilt temple; Persian peḥâ); Joel and Obadiah not explicitly chronological.
